query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coatings is primarily governed by the in‐situ formation of a uniform, self‐passivating tribo-oxide layer that is enabled by an equiatomic (balanced) elemental distribution. This uniform oxide film, which forms under sliding wear conditions, reinforces the coating’s hardness and reduces crack initiation, thereby minimizing the wear rate.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited, microwave-cladded equiatomic Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA protective coating on SS-304 steel with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Cu content from 20 wt% to a lower value (for example, 10 wt%) while correspondingly increasing one or more of the other elemental fractions to maintain a constant total, thus disturbing the equiatomic balance.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under controlled conditions (e.g., sliding speed of 2 m/s, load of 15 N, and sliding distance of 1000 m) at room temperature or elevated temperatures where tribo-oxidation is active. The modified coating is directly compared with the baseline equiatomic coating.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and uniformity of protective oxide phases (e.g., (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)_3O4) and the lattice distortion effect resulting from an even distribution of elements.
generation.mechanism: In an equiatomic HEA, the balanced elemental distribution promotes homogeneous nucleation and growth of a protective oxide during wear. This oxide layer acts as a self-healing barrier that reinforces hardness and suppresses micro-crack formation. Disrupting the balance (by reducing Cu) is hypothesized to lead to uneven oxide formation and a compromised barrier, which in turn increases the wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical wear test conditions, the baseline equiatomic coating will form a uniform oxide layer that yields a lower wear rate and relatively stable friction coefficient, whereas the Cu-reduced (modified) coating will exhibit a higher wear rate and more variable friction behavior due to an inhomogeneous oxide layer and increased microcracking.
generation.baseline: The performance of an equiatomic Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA coating on SS-304 steel as determined by previous studies (e.g., wear rate around 0.0018 mm³/m and a friction coefficient close to 0.2 under specified test conditions).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds for HEA protective coatings under wear conditions where tribo-oxidation plays a significant role, such as in applications with sliding contact in ambient or moderately high temperature environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative change in wear rate due to altering the Cu content may vary with the testing environment and the specific compensating adjustments in other element fractions. Additionally, other factors such as phase segregation or processing parameters could also impact oxide uniformity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings on SS-304 steel via the microwave cladding method: one using the baseline equiatomic composition (Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20) and one with a lowered Cu content (e.g., 10 wt% Cu with corresponding adjustments in the other elements). Subject both coatings to identical wear tests (e.g., sliding at 2 m/s, 15 N load, and 1000 m sliding distance) under conditions conducive to oxide formation.
measurements: Surface oxide layer morphology and uniformity (via SEM and EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified coating (with reduced Cu) exhibits wear performance metrics (wear rate, friction coefficient) and oxide layer characteristics that are statistically indistinguishable from those of the baseline equiatomic coating, then the hypothesis that the equiatomic balance enables a beneficial, uniform tribo-oxide layer governing wear performance would be falsified.

AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation. The microstructural characteristics of the AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings after the high temperature wear resistance test shows a highly favorable impact on microstructure stability and wear resistance, due to its the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetallic compounds.
